beyond_this_chapter.why: Nothing in this chapter showed that anything in an earlier chapter should read differently.

changes.find: Outside the door, grown dark at some point, was the sound of hard rain and wind.
changes.reason: `どこ`? No—the Japanese attaches the darkening to the place outside the door (`戸の外`), and `where` puts it there without attaching it to the door itself.
changes.replace: Outside the door, where it had grown dark at some point, was the sound of hard rain and wind.

changes.find: kept all their eyes upon the child.
changes.reason: `瞳を注いだ` takes the child—and `その子供のすべて`, all of her—as its object, not `all their eyes`, so the fix keeps the `all` where the Japanese puts it.
changes.replace: kept their eyes fixed on the child, on all of her.

changes.find: with fat, round hands short as balls,
changes.reason: `鞠のように短い` is a likeness (round hand-balls), and `like` restores that image while removing the unintended English slang of `short as balls`.
changes.replace: with fat round hands, short like balls,

changes.find: She dished out rice for him, hot and fresh from the pot with the white steam rising thick, and handed it to him.
changes.reason: After a paragraph centred on the father the bare pronoun strands the English reader, and the Japanese `彼女` here is unambiguously the mother serving, so naming her role resets the antecedent without adding information.
changes.replace: The mother dished out rice for him, hot and fresh from the pot with the white steam rising thick, and handed it to him.

changes.find: but the smile overflowed her face
changes.reason: The collocation needs a preposition, but the reading requires the laughter to stay `overflowing` (the p8–p9 exhaustion-laughter network), so the verb is kept and only the grammar repaired rather than replaced with `broke`.
changes.replace: but the smile overflowed across her face

changes.find: His eyes holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, he steadied the child
changes.reason: The `helplessly welled-up` smile is the text's (kept verbatim), but English eyes cannot hold a smile back; attaching the phrase to the father keeps the sense and the body where English can carry it.
changes.replace: Holding back the smile that welled up helplessly because of the child, he steadied the child

changes.find: In the gaps, hastily opening his own wide mouth, he stuffed rice into it.
changes.reason: `そのすきに` is `in that interval`—while his hands are busy with the child—and `in between` says which interval it is while keeping the hasty, crowded physicality of the feeding.
changes.replace: In between, hastily opening his own wide mouth, he shovelled rice into it.

changes.find: she chewed it over silently with her front teeth, but her heart had already bowed down in loneliness.
changes.reason: `Chewed it over` imports pondering the Japanese does not have (`前歯でかみなおした`, she bit at it again with her front teeth), and `sunk` gives `うつむいてしまっていた` an English life without a cooking cause or gloss.
changes.replace: she went on chewing silently with her front teeth, but her heart had already sunk in loneliness.

changes.find: with a far off heart she quietly remembered
changes.reason: The Japanese makes `遠い心が`—the far-off heart—the subject of `思い出している`, and restoring that subject is exactly the loosening of viewpoint the reading requires from p10 on; the reader's own suggested wording would have left it a fragment, so the smallest faithful form is used.
changes.replace: her far-off heart quietly remembered

changes.find: only went on quietly and peacefully smiling
changes.reason: `ぢっと` is the fixed, motionless quality on which the vision's stillness stands or falls, and `still` restores it in one dull word without disturbing the incantatory `quietly and peacefully ... did not move at all` that follows.
changes.replace: only went on quietly and peacefully, still smiling

changes.find: drew together with their heads together, telling a long story.
changes.reason: The doubled `together` is the translator's, not the author's—`より合って頭をあつめて` is drawing close and putting heads together—while the deliberate repetitions here are `long`, `quiet` and `smiling`, which are untouched.
changes.replace: drew close with heads together, telling a long story.

changes.find: And then they will be forever before a rest like night.
changes.reason: `夜のような安息` is a night-like rest, and moving the comparison into the adjective keeps `永久に...前にある` just as temporally unresolved as the Japanese while making the noun phrase grammatical English.
changes.replace: And then they will be forever before a night-like rest.

changes.find: The far picture lay dark and quiet in the bottom of her eyes.
changes.reason: `映っていた` is a picture reflected/seen, not lying, and the reading asks that the vision stay something seen and unresolved rather than a settled object.
changes.replace: The far picture was reflected dark and quiet in the bottom of her eyes.

changes.find: alone she gave a lonely, quiet sigh
changes.reason: `ひそかな` is secret/private, not `静か`; rendering it `quiet` collapses two words the text keeps distinct and erodes the `静か` network the reading protects.
changes.replace: alone she gave a lonely, secret sigh

changes.find: unable to say anything in a word she fell silent, and her eyes ran far away again.
changes.reason: `一口には言いかねて` is being unable to get it into a single utterance and `眼が遠く走った` is her gaze going far off; `put into words` and `gaze drifted` carry both without adding the psychology the narration withholds.
changes.replace: unable to put anything into words she fell silent, and her gaze drifted far away again.

changes.find: Really, only a very little time has passed since we married, hasn't it
changes.reason: `まだ` is present in both p22 and its return in p27 (`まだ三年しか経たない`), and the still/only-three-years repetition is the one sentence she brings back from the vision, so it must be whole in both places.
changes.replace: Still, really only a very little time has passed since we married, hasn't it

changes.find: But we have been through a lot, haven't we.
changes.reason: `いろいろ苦労した` is suffering undergone in many ways, and `been through a lot` is the flattening (Berman's impoverishment) that breaks the suffering/sorrow/weariness network the whole story is strung on.
changes.replace: But we have suffered in all sorts of ways, haven't we.

changes.find: two years are already past.
changes.reason: `二年はもう過ぎた` is elapsed time, and the perfect tense keeps the husband's practical forward counter-clock—the two years gone, the walking to come—grammatical and plain.
changes.replace: two years have already passed.

changes.find: Yes, we must work, mustn't we.
changes.reason: `働きましょうね` is a polite volitional—let's work—not an obligation, and the crux requires her return to be an ordinary resolution she agrees to, not a duty imposed or a resolve the narration invents.
changes.replace: Yes, let's work, shall we.

changes.find: Come, let us clear away. And sleep. Let us get up early tomorrow.
changes.reason: `片づけよう...寝よう...起きようじゃないか` is plain, tired, volitional speech, and contractions give it that register instead of a formal archaism the speaker nowhere else has.
changes.replace: Come, let's clear away. And sleep. Let's get up early tomorrow.

declined.reason: Declined: the clause after the quotation (`The young father stared...`) is an independent narrative sentence, not a dialogue tag, so a period inside the quotes with a capital following is correct English; forcing a comma and lower-case tag through p24–p38 would make action sentences ungrammatical, and the genuine tags in the chapter (`the man said`) are already correctly punctuated.

Declined: `彼女に静かな淋しい遠くはなれた心を与えた` deliberately gives her a heart, and that same far-off heart becomes the subject of the remembering in p13 (see F4); dissolving it into `a distant feeling` would break the detachment mechanism the reading names as the trigger and would vary `far` against the p10–p18 network, so the strangeness is the text's and stays.

Declined (see Disagreements): `眼の底` and then `瞳の底` repeat `bottom` within one sentence-pair, and that repetition is part of the text's wording, not an accident; `depths` is smoother English bought by erasing a repeated word, which the reading forbids, and with F3's `reflected` restored the sentence is already intelligible.

Declined: the Japanese says plainly `小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ始めた`—she put out a small nipple and began to nurse—and the reading explicitly warns against softening the ending into cosiness; `bared her breast` is the ennobled, vaguer version and would turn a plain bodily act into a tableau of mothering.

disagreements.choice: The faithful reader's side: F3 is taken (`was reflected ... in the bottom of her eyes`) and R13 is declined.
disagreements.faithful_side: F3: `映っていた` means the picture is reflected/seen in the bottom of her eyes, and `lay` loses that seeing.
disagreements.readable_side: R13: `bottom of her eyes` is not an English place and breaks the lingering picture; `depths of her eyes` would keep the dim-distance effect idiomatically.

data.say: Changes, declined notes, and the one disagreement (p18) are recorded above; nothing is sent up to the editor, since every reader disagreement in this chapter is settled by the house's reading.
